AUS.story:
In the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat, in Victoria, Bishop Ronald Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children. He kept appointing him to new parishes. Ridsdale was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children. In 2017 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, a national public inquiry with the power to require documents, called the bishop's decisions a "catastrophic" failure. It also found that in 1972 a senior police officer had offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating another Ballarat priest, Monsignor John Day.

In March 2008 the Adass Israel School in Melbourne paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. She was arrested in Israel in 2014. Her extradition, the legal handover of a suspect to another country, took until January 2021, partly because Israel's deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, interfered with her psychiatric assessments. She was convicted in Australia on 3 April 2023.

The Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017. It held 8,013 private sessions with survivors and heard evidence about 3,489 institutions. Of the survivors in those sessions, 58.1 percent had been abused in a religious institution and 32.5 percent in one run by government. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began in July 2018. Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the legal deadline for suing over child abuse.

A 1994 law let Australians be prosecuted at home for abusing children abroad. In 2016 about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas, 40 percent without telling police. In 2020 the bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty that included failing to check payments to the Philippines that could be linked to child exploitation.

Survivors abused in Australian institutions can now sue whenever the abuse happened. A 2020 study by International Justice Mission ranked Australians third among the buyers of abuse streamed live from the Philippines.

NZL.story:
In 2018 New Zealand set up the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, a public inquiry into what happened to children and adults placed in state and church care. Its final report, in July 2024, estimated that 200,000 of the roughly 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 had been abused, and that sexual abuse was commonplace. Māori were more likely to be abused. The commissioners found that the state had not responded to signs of systemic abuse, and that by 2024 little had been done on the redress system they had recommended in 2021.

Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital, about half of them Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks given without anaesthetic as punishment, and evidence was given of children raped by staff and adult patients. The psychiatrist in charge, Selwyn Leeks, denied abuse and was never charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission found that many of the children had been tortured, and in December 2024 the government offered each survivor NZ$150,000 and a new apology.

In church care, the commission found that abusers were moved to other posts where they offended again. At Marylands, a Christchurch school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended between 1955 and 1984 reported abuse, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served there faced allegations. After allegations against Brother Bernard McGrath in 1977, the order moved him to Australia; he was later put in charge of its Hebron Trust in Christchurch and has since been convicted of more than 100 offences in the two countries. The commission recommended an inquiry into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations.

New Zealand now has a full count of abuse in care, and Lake Alice survivors have been offered payments. Most other survivors are still waiting for the redress system the commission asked for.

ESP.story:
After the Civil War of 1936 to 1939, the Franco government placed about 30,000 children in state care. A 2008 ruling by Judge Baltasar Garzón described most of them as children whose parents were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding or disappeared. Their names were changed so they could be given to families who supported the regime. Unmarried mothers held in homes run by the Women's Protection Board, a state body, were also pressured to give up their babies, and this continued into the early 1980s. The 1977 Amnesty Law, which barred prosecution for crimes of the dictatorship, made these removals hard to investigate, and many of the Board's files went missing in 1996.

In 2011 families of 261 babies who had disappeared from Spanish hospitals asked the attorney general to investigate an alleged network of doctors and nurses, and lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies had been taken. The first trial, of Dr Eduardo Vela in 2018, ended in acquittal because the legal deadline for prosecution had passed. In 2026 forensic geneticists at Spain's National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences found no evidence of systematic theft from hospitals and called the 300,000 figure a hoax, while not disputing the coercion in Francoist institutions.

The Catholic Church was examined later. On 27 October 2023 the Ombudsman, Ángel Gabilondo, presented Spain's first official inquiry into abuse in the church to parliament, based on 487 cases. It said the church had often minimised or denied the problem. In a survey of about 8,000 adults for the report, 11.7 percent said they had been abused before 18, 1.13 percent by clergy or lay church members and 0.6 percent by clergy. Gabilondo did not turn these percentages into a total; newspapers that did put it at about 440,000, and the bishops apologised but disputed that figure.

How many children Franco's institutions took and where they went is still unsettled, and the amnesty law still stands in the way of prosecutions. The church inquiry gave Spain its first survey-based estimate of abuse by clergy.

MEX.story:
In 1941 the priest Marcial Maciel founded the Legion of Christ, a Catholic religious order, in Mexico. Former seminarians wrote to the Vatican about his abuse in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and filed formal charges in 1998, without result. In 2010 the Vatican said his acts were "true crimes" and that the Legion had shielded him. He was never tried. In 2019 the Legion's own report found that 33 of its priests had abused 175 minors since 1941, at least 60 of them abused by Maciel.

In 2003 several girls in Cancún complained about the hotel owner Jean Succar Kuri, who was detained in the United States in 2004 and sent back. In 2005 the journalist Lydia Cacho published a book linking him to the Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and the Puebla governor, Mario Marín. Puebla state police then arrested Cacho in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla, and she says she was tortured. Leaked phone calls recorded the two men discussing jailing her as a favour. In 2007 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6 to 4 that Marín had no case to answer. Succar Kuri was convicted in 2011 and died in 2024 while serving his sentence. Marín was arrested in 2021 on torture charges and his trial continues; neither he nor Nacif has been convicted.

When federal police raided the La Gran Familia shelter in Zamora in 2014 they freed 432 children, some of whom had been sexually abused; more than 40 complaints from parents had reached state and federal authorities before the raid. In 2009, 14 children disappeared from Casitas del Sur, a church-run shelter in Mexico City where city prosecutors had placed them.

In 2020 Mexico's bishops said they had investigated 426 priests over ten years and removed 217. The newspaper El Universal found that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such offences by religious figures between 2009 and 2019, and four prosecutors' offices recorded six convictions.

Most abuse reported in Mexican churches and shelters has not reached a court, and the torture trial over Cacho's arrest is still not finished.

RUS.story:
From the 1990s Russia sent large numbers of children from its orphanages to families abroad. The United States issued visas to 60,266 children adopted from Russia between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 5,865, in 2004. In 2010 an American adoptive mother sent her 7-year-old adopted son back to Moscow alone on a one-way flight, and Russian officials called for adoptions by Americans to stop. On 28 December 2012 President Vladimir Putin signed the Dima Yakovlev Law, which banned adoption by US citizens from 2013. It was named after a Russian toddler who died in an American family's car, and it was widely seen as a response to a US law, the Magnitsky Act, signed two weeks earlier.

In 2014 Human Rights Watch visited 10 state orphanages for children with disabilities and found staff beating children, injecting them with sedatives and tying some to furniture. It reported that health workers pressured parents to give up children with disabilities.

After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, it began moving Ukrainian children from occupied areas into Russia. In May 2022 Putin signed a decree making it easier to give these children Russian citizenship so Russian families could adopt them, and the state paid families for each child. Researchers at Yale found at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for "re-education". On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and for Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's children's rights commissioner, for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Ukraine counts 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced and 2,752 returned by October 2026.

Russia remains closed to American adopters, and most of the Ukrainian children it took have not been returned. The UN says the whereabouts of most of the 122 abductions it verified are still unknown.

NOR.story:
Between 1955 and 2008 Norway received 6,295 children for adoption from South Korea. In 1974 and 1975, when South Korea tried to stop sending children abroad, Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to continue. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body that investigates past abuses, found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, registered children who had known parents as orphans and did not properly obtain consent. It said the Korean state had failed to supervise them.

Norway opened its own investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions, the adoption of children from abroad, and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them. The foreign ministry said it was aware of serious findings. In September 2025 a woman adopted from Korea gave notice that she would sue the Norwegian state, alleging that her adoption was illegal.

Children in Norway's own institutions had been examined earlier. An official report in 2004, NOU 2004:23, found neglect and abuse, including sexual abuse, in municipal children's homes and state special schools between 1945 and 1980. In 2005 a committee of the Storting, the parliament, recommended a state compensation scheme with payments of up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof, and Bergen and other municipalities set up their own schemes.

In 2026, after US authorities released documents about Jeffrey Epstein, Norway's economic crime agency charged the former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland with aggravated corruption, examining whether he received gifts, travel and loans in connection with his position. He denies the charges, and the case concerns corruption, not abuse.

Norway has paid compensation to people abused in its children's homes. What its own officials knew about the adoptions from Korea is still under investigation.

LKA.story:
In the 1980s thousands of Sri Lankan babies were adopted by families abroad, about 4,000 of them in the Netherlands and others in Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. Babies were bought, or taken from hospitals, and handed to paid "acting mothers", who posed as the birth mothers in court; brokers and some hospital doctors and nurses acted as intermediaries for Western agencies. In 1987 police raided one of these "baby farms" and found 20 newborns and 22 women held in prison-like conditions, and Sri Lanka temporarily stopped foreign adoptions. In 2017, after a Dutch television documentary, the health minister, Rajitha Senaratne, admitted that there had been "a lot of baby farms" and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank for families searching for each other. In 2021 a Dutch government committee found that officials had known of the abuses for years without acting, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption. Switzerland's government acknowledged its authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023.

Sri Lankan soldiers served in Haiti with MINUSTAH, the UN peacekeeping mission there. The UN's internal investigators found that between 2004 and 2007 members of the Sri Lankan contingent sexually exploited and abused children frequently and at almost every place they were posted. In 2007, 114 were accused and 108 were sent home. Under UN rules only the soldiers' own country can prosecute them, and Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts "consensual". No one was jailed, and one victim received a one-off payment in 2016.

Inside Sri Lanka, complaints about a children's home in Vavuniya, run by a Buddhist monk and housing children affected by the war, reached the National Child Protection Authority from 2010. The monk was arrested in 2013 for abusing a 9-year-old, and was released on bail after the Authority said it did not object.

No Sri Lankan soldier has been jailed for the abuse in Haiti. South Asia has no representative survey data on online abuse of children, so how common it is in Sri Lanka is not known.

AUT.story:
In 1995 Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, the Catholic Archbishop of Vienna, stepped down after a former pupil, and then others, accused him of sexual abuse. In 1998 the Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded. After a wave of new disclosures in 2010, the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission, chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, to decide on payments to people abused in the church. It paid in tiers of €5,000, €15,000 and €25,000, with more in extreme cases, and by August 2021 payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. In 2013 a court jailed the former head of the boarding school at Kremsmünster Abbey for 12 years for crimes against 24 former pupils.

The City of Vienna examined its own children's home at Wilhelminenberg, which it ran from 1948 to 1977. A commission it appointed interviewed 217 people, including 140 former residents, and reported in 2013 that children there had been raped and sexually exploited by caregivers and by men from outside, some girls as young as about six. It found that staff in the city department responsible knew of the abuse and did nothing, and that city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it. Its findings were sent to prosecutors, and some former residents received up to €35,000.

Austria has also been a starting point for international investigations of online abuse. In 2006 an employee of a Vienna file-hosting company reported suspicious material, and within a day investigators recorded visits from 2,361 internet addresses in 77 countries. In 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being abused.

In Austria most payments to people abused as children were set by commissions, one created by the church and one by the city of Vienna. The Wilhelminenberg findings reached prosecutors more than 35 years after the home closed.

GTM.story:
After Guatemala's civil war ended in 1996, adoptions of Guatemalan children by foreigners rose every year. About 98 percent were handled by private notaries, lawyers who arranged both sides of the adoption without review by a court and charged $35,000 or more per child. Almost all the children, 97 percent, went to the United States, which issued visas to 32,863 children adopted from Guatemala between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 4,728, in 2007. In August 2007 police found 46 children at Casa Quivira, a private adoption home in Antigua, after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children every day. The attorney general said most lacked proper documents and that his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or taken from mothers under pressure.

In December 2007 Guatemala passed a law following the Hague Convention, the international treaty that sets safeguards for adoptions between countries, and stopped new adoptions to the United States from January 2008. In 2010 CICIG, a UN-backed commission investigating crime in Guatemala, studied 153 adoption cases and found that 78 percent broke the law in some way.

Children in state care were also at risk. About 700 children lived in the Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, a state home built for 500, and most had committed no crime. Prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, girls had alleged sexual abuse by staff, and in 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman reported a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On 8 March 2017, after an escape, police locked a group of girls in a room; one set a mattress on fire, and 41 girls died. In August 2025 a judge convicted six former officials, including the former social welfare secretary, who received 25 years, and said the fire followed abuses that had been reported and not acted on.

International adoption from Guatemala has been closed since 2008. Officials responsible for the state home have been convicted, and the judge ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.

PER.story:
In 1971 Luis Fernando Figari founded the Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana, a Catholic lay society, in Lima. In 2015 the journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz published a book describing abuse by Figari and those around him, and they then faced legal action. The Vatican appointed an official to examine the group the same year. In 2017 the society gave Peruvian prosecutors an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred him from contact with members. After a further Vatican investigation, Figari was expelled in August 2024 for physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors, and the society was formally dissolved in 2025.

Religious orders also moved abusers into and out of Peru. In 2010 Brother Abel Pérez of the Marist Brothers, a teaching order, confessed to his superiors in Chile that he had abused minors, and the order transferred him to Peru; in 2017 it acknowledged at least 14 victims. In the other direction, the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas first abused a child in Lima in 1964, then moved to Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools.

Children are also exploited in places where the state has little control. In 2019 more than 1,500 soldiers and police moved against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in Madre de Dios, and the women's minister said child sexual exploitation had been among the worst crimes there. In 2021 a 16-year-old girl who had earlier been rescued from a trafficking group in La Pampa was found murdered. The US State Department reported in 2025 that tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon, and that in Loreto criminal groups take tourists by boat to remote places on the river where women and children are exploited.

The Sodalicio no longer exists, and its founder has been expelled by the church but not convicted by a Peruvian court. Exploitation of children in mining camps and by tourists continues.
